extracted.intended_audience: young mathematicians, graduate students, and early-career researchers considering tackling major open problems
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for mathematicians about when (and when not) to devote research time to a single large open problem or grand unifying theory, and a checklist of questions to ask before publishing claimed solutions to famous problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t prematurely obsess on a single big problem or big theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid becoming focused, to the exclusion of other mathematical activity, on a single really difficult problem in a field (or on some grand unifying theory) before one is really ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a 'particularly dangerous occupational hazard' especially if one has not yet learnt the limitations of one’s tools or acquired a healthy scepticism of one’s own work; neglecting other tasks (writing and publishing lesser results) in hope of a big payoff is a strong warning sign to rebalance priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spend most time on feasible 'low-hanging fruit' until ready
rubrics_metrics.description: If ideas for big problems still have a significant speculative component (or the grand theory lacks a definite striking application), keep the big problems in mind but tinker occasionally while focusing most effort on more feasible work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working on low-hanging fruit builds experience, mathematical power, and credibility for later tackling ambitious projects; do not rely on an eventual single big payoff to compensate for lack of steady progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconditions before betting reputational capital
rubrics_metrics.description: One should generally have (1) a proven track record of reliably producing significant papers in the area already, and (2) a secure career (e.g. a tenured position) before devoting most research time to a high-risk big problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without both a track record and career security, the obsessive route has seldom worked well; failing to meet these is an explicit warning against spending one's reputational capital on speculative big-picture work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the limitations of your tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of the known limits of your methods and avoid pushing a method beyond its known limits without understanding why obstructions might occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many high-profile erroneous claims arise from pushing a method well beyond its known limits and encountering obstructions known to experts; know and state potential limitations in the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire and exercise healthy scepticism of your own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Be extraordinarily sceptical of claims of major breakthroughs and exercise utmost care and caution before releasing such work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately try to disprove or hunt for errors in the paper; avoid rushing; if errors are quickly found after public release, reputational damage can follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and emphasise the key new idea or insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly state 'What is the key new idea or insight? How does it differ from what has been tried before?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This idea should be emphasised in the introduction (the author asks: 'Where's the beef?'). A clear statement helps readers and referees judge novelty and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain relation to earlier partial results or attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss how the arguments relate to earlier partial results or attempts and whether there are clear analogues between steps here and previous papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address whether the new work sheds light on why previous approaches did not fully succeed; omission of this context is a negative sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the simplest, shortest, or clearest new application (proof-of-concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the first non-trivial new statement enabled by the idea and its proof, rather than jumping straight to the full big conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a fatal error exists in the full proof, a deep and non-trivial new partial result is often salvageable; show a concrete proof-of-concept in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address known counterexamples, obstructions, and philosophical objections
rubrics_metrics.description: For any major problem, list known counterexamples or obstructions to classes of attack and explain why your argument does not encounter these obstructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State specific limitations of the argument in the paper as well; failure to do so is a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the high-level strategy and heuristics guiding the attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the high-level strategy, heuristics, or intuition behind the argument in rising-above-technical-terms language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the strategy is merely 'continue blindly transforming the problem until a miracle occurs', this is particularly bad; the paper should be able to state why the argument works at a conceptual level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify key milestones or intermediate results
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof come with key milestones—such as a key proposition of independent interest or a major reduction of the problem to a significantly easier one?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly identify and highlight these milestones in the paper; they provide evidence of substantive progress even if the full claim is flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate robustness of the argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how fragile the argument is: could a single sign error or illegal step destroy the entire proof?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good indicators of robustness include alternate proofs, heuristics, supporting examples of key steps, or analogies with other literature; fragile, miracle-based chains are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check the paper critically and rework exposition thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly check the paper for errors and rework the exposition before release; do not rush publication of a claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately try to find mistakes; take extra days to go through the paper one last time—there is usually no rush for a major problem that has resisted solutions for years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance routine background and new material appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how much space is devoted to routine theory and computations already in previous literature versus the new material; ensure new material appears early and is given appropriate detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid burying the new ideas deep inside routine exposition; show the new stuff as soon as possible and allocate detail sensibly between background and novel contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bragging or self-promoting titles and introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep any bragging or self-promoting text with little informative mathematical content to a minimum in the title, abstract, and introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of a bad title: 'A proof of the Poincaré conjecture'. Example of a good title: 'The entropy formula for the Ricci flow and its geometric applications'. Do not overstate the obvious historical importance of the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for hostile reception without auxiliary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Most professional mathematicians will refuse to read further attempts on famous problems unless there is substantial auxiliary evidence that there is a non-zero chance of correctness (e.g. a previous track record).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide auxiliary evidence (track record, intermediate results, convincing heuristics) to increase the chance the community will engage with the manuscript; see editorial policies referenced for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and community-policy awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of journal/editorial policies and community norms regarding papers that claim solutions to famous problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao references his own editorial policy and links such as Oded Goldreich’s page and discussions like Scott Aaronson's 'Ten signs a claimed mathematical proof is wrong' and Dick Lipton's 'On Mathematical Diseases' as further context and cautionary material.
